title: The Solar System
summary: The sun, the eight planets and other bodies in the solar system, gravity and orbits, the Earth–Moon system, phases of the moon, eclipses and tides.

notes.text: The **solar system** is made up of the **sun** and everything that orbits it: eight planets and their moons, dwarf planets such as Pluto, asteroids, comets and meteoroids. The sun is a **star**: a huge ball of hot hydrogen and helium gas that produces energy by **nuclear fusion**. It contains more than 99% of the mass of the solar system.

notes.caption: Planets in order from the sun
rows: Smallest planet; closest to the sun; no moons
Hottest planet because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat
Only known planet with liquid water on the surface and life
The red planet, coloured by iron oxide dust; two small moons
Largest planet; the Great Red Spot is a giant storm
Famous for its bright rings of ice and rock
Furthest from the sun; strongest winds in the solar system

notes.label: Memory aid
notes.text: **M**y **V**ery **E**ager **M**other **J**ust **S**erved **U**s **N**achos: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
The **asteroid belt**, a ring of rocky bodies, lies between Mars and Jupiter and separates the inner rocky planets from the outer giant planets.

items: **Comets**: balls of ice and dust with long, very elliptical orbits; near the sun they form a glowing tail that points away from the sun.
**Meteoroids**: small pieces of rock in space. A **meteor** (shooting star) is one burning up in our atmosphere; a **meteorite** is one that reaches the ground.

notes.text: **Gravity** is the force of attraction between all objects with mass. The sun's gravity keeps the planets moving in almost circular paths called **orbits**. The Earth's gravity keeps the moon in orbit around the Earth and pulls objects towards the ground.

rows: One year; together with the tilt of the axis, the seasons
About 27,3 days (29,5 days from one full moon to the next)

notes.text: The moon does not produce its own light; it reflects light from the sun. Half of the moon is always lit by the sun, but as it orbits the Earth we see different amounts of the lit half. The sequence is: new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → **full moon** → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: The same side of the moon always faces the Earth, because the moon spins once on its axis in the same time that it takes to orbit the Earth once.

rows: The moon's shadow falls on Earth and blocks the sun (at new moon). Never look directly at the sun.
The Earth's shadow falls on the moon, which may look dark red (at full moon).

notes.text: **Tides** are the regular rise and fall of the sea, caused mainly by the moon's gravity pulling on the oceans. Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day. **Spring tides** (biggest range) happen at new and full moon, when the sun and moon pull in a line; **neap tides** (smallest range) happen at the quarter moons.
